segmenti.tekst: جدد حياة القلب بالقرآن كي تطمئن الروح بالإيمان. إن الحمد لله نحمده ونستعينه ونستغفره، ونعوذ بالله من شرور أنفسنا ومن سيئات أعمالنا، من يهده الله فلا مضل له ومن يضلل فلا هادي له، وأشهد أن لا إله إلا الله وحده لا شريك له، وأشهد أن محمدا عبده ورسوله، أرسله الله تبارك وتعالى بالهدى ودين الحق،

لينذر من كان حيا ويحق القول على الكافرين، صلوات ربي وسلامه عليه وعلى الصحابة والتابعين ومن تبعهم بإحسان إلى يوم الدين. Dear and respected brothers, honoured members of the congregation, honoured believers, first of all, boundless praise be to Allah the Exalted, the Lord of all the worlds, the Master of the Day of Judgement, the Most Gracious and Most Merciful, for making us adherents of the only religion recognised by Him, the religion of Islam.

Praise be to Him for granting us the noble Qur'an as guidance for us in our lives, and praise be to Him for sending us the Prophet Muhammad, sallallahu alayhi wa sallam (peace be upon him), His most chosen creation and the last Messenger, so that he should be our Prophet and our role model and we his ummah; under his banner we live, and under his banner we will be resurrected on the Day of Judgement.

Dear and respected brothers, honoured believers, adherents of Islam, how aware are we of the blessing that Allah, jalla sha'nuhu (exalted is His majesty), has given us by making us followers of His noble religion? By letting us be born as Muslims and by guiding us in our lives to grasp the truth before we depart to the next world.

That is the greatest blessing anyone can receive: guidance, belonging to Islam, holding fast to the din of Islam; to belong to Islam completely, to belong to Islam and to be a follower of the Prophet Muhammad, sallallahu alayhi wa sallam, and through that to earn barakah (blessing) and the pleasure of Allah, jalla sha'nuhu, in this world, and the eternal reward, Jannah (Paradise), in the world to come.

There is no better reward, no better ni'mah, no better blessing that Allah, jalla sha'nuhu, could have given you than this. So however things go for you in this world, for you and for me, whatever trials you face, if you preserve and perfect this blessing, good is surely written for you.

Surely good in this world, and most surely good, eternal good, in the world to come. However, Allah, jalla sha'nuhu, says in the Qur'an, addressing us, addressing all people and especially the believers: "O you who believe," or "O people, enter into the religion completely" – enter into the religion completely, and all of you completely, and even if we enter individually, let us enter into the religion completely and accept it completely, and by no means divide it, taking from the religion what we like and rejecting from the religion what we do not like.

Accepting what is easy for us and rejecting what is hard for us. Rather, we should enter into the religion absolutely and completely, accepting every religious principle and letting every religious tenet enter our hearts and fill every pore of our worldly life.

Let it enter every segment of our life. Let it fill our day from the morning until we lie down in the evening. For religion is not just for the mosque, and religion is not just for at home either. Religion is for every time and every place.

Religion is something that is with you from the moment you open your eyes until you lose consciousness in the evening, when you lie down again to sleep. Religion is something that should accompany you from the first day you came into this world until the last moment, until you leave this world. And religion is something that must absolutely and completely take hold of and fill your mind, your reason and your soul, your heart.

Religion is not something we should play around with, taking only part of it and discarding other parts. What makes us Muslims, dear and respected brothers? What makes us Muslims, first of all, is iman, the faith we carry in our hearts.

When we say faith here, we mean the true faith that a person carries in his heart, that he knows and believes in everything he has been prescribed to believe. And we all know the six articles of iman. And we all, we hope, learned them in the mekteb (Qur'an school); if we have not, we must renew them.

And that is to believe in Allah – "amantu billahi" – "wa mala'ikatihi" – and in His angels – "wa kutubihi" – and in His books – "wa rusulihi" – and in His messengers, and that everything that happens comes about by Allah's qadar, His decree, whether it be good or evil.

And these are the tenets below which there is no minimum. This is the minimum that brings us into the faith. That is why a person who is not a Muslim, when he enters the din of Islam, if he does not believe in these six tenets, however much he pronounces the shahadah, it is not accepted from him.

It is not accepted from him; rather, he must believe in these six tenets, then pronounce the shahadah, and then become a true believer, a believer in his heart. And we Muslims believe. And that is the basis of our faith, which is in our hearts. For we firmly believe in these six tenets: we believe in Allah, we believe in angels and jinn, we believe in the messengers, we believe in the books that Allah, jalla sha'nuhu, revealed, we believe in the Day of Judgement and we believe in qadar, in the decree of Allah, jalla sha'nuhu, in destiny.

Next, what makes us Muslims is practice, which in the books of Shari'ah is called islam. These are the Islamic duties to which we are strictly bound. In both the first and the second there are obligatory elements and those that are not obligatory.

In iman, these six are obligatory, and beyond that we should believe in every ayah of the Qur'an and in everything that the Prophet Muhammad, sallallahu alayhi wa sallam, brought. And among the Islamic pillars, five are obligatory, and they are, after the shahadah, prayer, then fasting, zakat and Hajj – something that is a strict obligation for every Muslim.

These five pillars are a strict obligation for every Muslim. A strict obligation: prayer, all five daily prayers, the fard prayers, and the fast of the month of Ramadan, and zakat as it is prescribed, and Hajj if a person is able to go.

A strict obligation for every Muslim. And that too makes us Muslims, the practice by which we practise the religion of Islam. However, Islam does not stop there. And what we have mentioned, I assume, is very clear to all of us, and we are all, I hope, practising it, or intend to put it into practice soon.

So if we are not able to go on Hajj now and not able to give zakat now, if we are not obliged, we surely intend to fulfil all these five pillars of the din of Islam at the first opportunity that arises. However, our din of Islam does not stop here. The din of Islam is not only what you carry in your heart, although that is the main thing.

The din of Islam is not only how you practise the religion in the mosque and how you practise the rites and these ritual obligations of the din of Islam, although that is something that makes us Muslims and is obligatory, but it is not only that. Allah, jalla sha'nuhu, has also prescribed ihsan for us, as the third and highest level of the religion, which is also obligatory for Muslims at its minimum.

Which is also obligatory. And what is ihsan? As the Prophet Muhammad, sallallahu alayhi wa sallam, says, it is that you worship Allah as though you see Him, for if you do not see Him, He sees you. Ihsan is the perfecting of every deed. Ihsan is that you perfect every possible deed that you do.

That you do it purely for the sake of Allah. That is the obligation of each one of us. That is the minimum of ihsan: that everything you do, you do for the sake of Allah. And that you bring the deed you do to perfection, as far as you are able. That when you come to prayer, you bring that prayer to perfection.

That when you go home, you bring your relationship with your family to perfection, with your parents, the members of your household, the young and the old, and so on. Then the Prophet Muhammad, sallallahu alayhi wa sallam, in the context of ihsan, says something that also falls under ihsan,

under the obligatory, the obligatory part of ihsan, on which we place the emphasis of today's hutba (Friday sermon). He says: "Man tashabbaha bi qawmin fa huwa minhum." He says: whoever follows, imitates, emulates a people belongs to them.

What does the Prophet mean by this? Whoever imitates some non-Muslim people belongs to them, that is, he is not one of us Muslims. Whoever imitates a people that is not Muslim is not one of us Muslims. So the Prophet strictly forbids imitating other peoples.

And this too is part of ihsan, because this is our cultural and declared belonging to Islam. Something that is obligatory for every Muslim, and that is that culturally, in every sense, he belongs to the din of Islam. That is why Muslims always, throughout history, to this very day – even though, with today's Western civilisation and globalisation, which devours all cultures, not only the Islamic one, this has become badly corrupted today – but even today, even today this must be present.

And that is that you are a Muslim in every pore of your life. When you go out into the street, you visibly belong to Islam. That whoever meets you in the street knows that you are a Muslim. By what? By your appearance, by your nur (light), by your nur, by the beard that is prescribed, by every possible feature of a Muslim's appearance; that the clothes you wear, whatever they may be, are Islamic, that they are in accordance with the Shari'ah, that they are not contrary to the Shari'ah; that the trousers you, as a Muslim man, have put on are Muslim, that they are not tight, or, Allah forbid, ripped, so that you resemble another people that is not Islamic.

Yes, especially when it comes to a Muslim woman: when she goes out into the street, let her be a true Muslim woman, let her genuinely and truly belong to Islam culturally. Because that is our strict obligation. A strict obligation for all of us, about which we will be asked, both you and I.

For we are shepherds in our families. Each of you, and each of us, is a shepherd in his family, and will be asked about what they do. Do we belong to Islam, and does a person who comes from outside, when he walks through our streets, say: "This is a Muslim place"? When he enters our čaršija (old town bazaar), does he say: "This is a Muslim čaršija"?

That is our obligation. It is our obligation that visually, as individuals, as families and as town quarters, we look Muslim. That we look Muslim and that Islamic culture is clearly seen in the outlines of our towns, our houses, our families and in ourselves.

And that we belong to Islamic civilisation. Next, in your speech you must be an adherent of Islam. There cannot be on your tongue and in your speech something that belongs to a people that is not Muslim. What should we put as number one here? Number one: the salam.

Why do the Muslims in Novi Pazar, where they are the majority, not greet one another with salam when they meet? Why, when you call your mother or your brother, is "As-salamu alaykum" not the first thing heard from you? Why, when you enter a shop or anywhere else, and you know that the person opposite you is a Muslim, do you not say "As-salamu alaykum"?

Why, when you enter a state institution, any one at all, and you know that the person opposite you, at least one of them, is a Muslim – "As-salamu alaykum" must be heard from you. Why? Because it is one of the tenets of cultural belonging to Islam. Something you must be proud of and something you must put into practice.

When the Prophet Muhammad, sallallahu alayhi wa sallam, entered Medina, one of the companions says, he went to see him. He had not even reached Medina yet; he had only just come to Quba'. Those who have been on Hajj know where Quba' is. The Prophet had not yet reached Medina; he would only come to Medina some fifteen days later.

But he had drawn near to Medina and arrived. The inhabitants found out that the Prophet had come. And this companion says: I approached the Prophet; people had gathered around him. He did not say "pray," nor "fast"; rather, he said: "Ayyuhan-nas, afshus-salam."

O people, spread the salam. Spread the salam – why? Because the salam is the banner of Islam. Why? Because the salam is the basic marker of our identity. The basic marker of our identity is the salam. If you have not established the salam in your family, by Allah, you are very sinful.

You are very sinful, and you owe a great debt to your family, whether to the younger ones, especially the younger ones, but also the older ones. If you have not established the salam in your family, if the salam is not heard under your roof, you owe a great debt and you are in great sin. And it is questionable how much Islam is in your heart.

How much you have allowed and opened the door for Islam to enter your heart. Islam is rushing towards us, but we are blocking it. We close our hearts to Islam. Islam is rushing to illuminate our minds, to enlighten our lives, to bring barakah into our homes, to bring barakah into our lives.

We are blocking it, because we take a part and reject a part. We are blocking it. Do not allow that, dear brother; rather, open the door wide to Islam. Let Islam enter your home. Let it, above all, enter every pore of your life.

Put the salam into practice, put every tenet of Islam into practice, and you will find great barakah in this world, and an immense barakah in the world to come. And do not pay attention to what people will say. Rather, go in and give the salam. Go in and give the salam; let it be seen that you are a Muslim.

Do not be ashamed of it; rather, be proud of your identity. Allah forbid that in the house of someone who prays one should hear "ciao," or any other greeting that does not belong to us. Ours is only "As-salamu alaykum," "merhaba," "Allahimanet" (go with Allah's protection), and so on. These are our cultural markers. Everything else does not belong to us.

Look at how much other peoples take care of these things. But we, from wherever the wind blows, are ready to accept it, from anyone's side, from the east and from the west. Whatever blows our way, we accept it. No, let us hold on to what is ours and be proud of what is ours.

Next, also part of belonging to Islam through language is that you preserve your people's language as it is, that you preserve the language of your father and your grandfather as you should. You do not have to speak pure standard Bosnian – that is not part of our language in Novi Pazar and in this part of the Sandžak.

But preserve the language of your father. Do not let "lepo," "belo" and "mleko" (the ekavian forms of "lijepo," "bijelo" and "mlijeko") enter your speech. Why would you? Did your father and your grandfather speak like that? Certainly not. Neither mine nor yours. Yet you have allowed it to yourself and the members of your household, especially among the women, who really do mix it up when it comes to this.

Especially those who work in state institutions. And especially, too, when you go into a shop – you go into a shop and she asks you: "Do you want 'mleko', or will you take 'dve'?" and so on. That is not our language. Where is that language from?

It is strange to me. At my thirty-something years, it is strange to me. Let alone to those who are older? Strange, I am not used to it. Let alone those who are older – they are not used to that language. They are not used to that language. Do not allow it for yourself, your household and those around you.

Feel free to point it out: where did you get that language from? Who imposed it on you? Throughout our schooling, throughout our education, a foreign language was imposed on us. And we allowed ourselves to be ashamed of our own language, to be ashamed of the language of our fathers and grandfathers. Why would we do that?

Why would we do that? Be proud of your language. Because that is part of cultural belonging to Islam, and it is part of your iman and your faith, that you are distinct from a people that is not Muslim.

Once, when to a caliph – and with this we will conclude – once, when Christian Arabs came to a caliph, who were Arabs but were Christians, even before Islam they had been a Christian, well, a Christian Arab tribe, they said: "O caliph" – this concerns Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz, one of the best-known, best and most just caliphs – they said: "O caliph, return us to the Arabs."

And the caliph said: "Are you not," he said, "Arabs?" They said: "We are, but we are," he says, "Christians," and the Muslims had forbidden them to grow their hair long. For it was the custom of the Arabs to grow their hair long. And since all the Arabs except them had accepted Islam, the Muslim rulers forbade them to grow their hair long, so that they would be distinguished from the Muslims.

Only so that they would be distinguished from the Muslims. And they asked the caliph to allow them to grow their hair long, because that was their Arab custom. They said: "Return us to the Arabs, allow us to grow our hair long." He said: "But are you not," he said, "Arabs?" They said: "We are, but we are Christians." "Well," he said, "that is not possible. Bring me scissors. It is not possible. You must be distinguished."

And that is why we Muslims must be distinguished from the Christians. And we must be distinguished from the people alongside whom we live, with whom we live, to whom we wish no harm at all, but we must be distinguished, taking pride in our origins, for we truly have nothing to be ashamed of. We have nothing to be ashamed of. On the contrary, we are a people with a great many reasons to be proud – the nobility of the Balkans, whose heirs we are, only we have forgotten it.

I ask Allah, jalla sha'nuhu, to have mercy on us, to grant us every khayr (good), to allow us to be proud of Islam and to let Muslims be proud of us as part of their ummah; that Allah, jalla sha'nuhu, may allow us to raise the banner of Islam high and proudly, not to be ashamed of any tenet of Islam, to carry the banner we bear and the burning ember of Islam that scorches our hands as it should be carried, to hand it on to future generations, who will raise it even higher and make Islam in these lands even prouder, and that Allah, jalla sha'nuhu, may be pleased with us and with our ancestors and descendants, and that until the Day of Judgement the adhan may be heard from our mosques
and Islam be proudly practised.
